newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German leaders say working to meet euro criteria.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German leaders say working to meet euro criteria.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl led a chorus of German officials on Tuesday in reassuring the German public and jittery markets that Germany would meet the deficit criterion for European economic and monetary union (EMU).

Kohl, answering critics who say the euro should be delayed rather than introduced if the fiscal criteria are not met, said Germany's budget deficit would achieve the strict target of 3.0 percent of gross domestic product in 1997 and 1998.

"We are sticking to three-point-zero. That is no problem. And with the schedule," Kohl said at an entrepreneurs' conference in Munich. He added that the critics who seek a delay in EMU are making an error, and the timetable should be adhered to.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel said the German government was working tirelessly to meet the criteria for Europe's single currency and said reaching the fiscal targets was more important than the timetable.

Speaking at an international monetary conference in Frankfurt, Waigel said Germany intended to meet the criteria for EMU entry in the short and long term and there could be no automatic entry for any country.
"Germany will do everything to meet the criteria now and forever," he said in a panel discussion at Global 24, a conference on EMU which linked participants across the globe with a video link-up.
"There can be no automatic entry for any country to EMU and no automatic exclusions."
Germany like other nations is currently having difficulties meeting the criteria, struggling both with a high budget deficit and a high debt ratio.
EMU's guiding Maastricht Treaty states that countries must meet targets on these fiscal criteria as well as on interest rates, exchange rates and inflation.

Kohl had planned to deliver a hard-hitting speech in Munich in which was going to include pointed criticism of Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber, whose frequent expressions of doubts about the euro have caused tension within Kohl's centre-right coalition government.

But after Stoiber praised an assurance Kohl made on Monday evening about the criteria for the euro not being watered down, the chancellor scrapped the original speech in which he was to say that said the euro discussion was "not helpful."

Stoiber is a leader in the Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party to Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU). Stoiber has been sniping at his coalition partners, pressing for strict implementation of the EMU criteria.
Stoiber said he welcomed Kohl's remark that the deficit rule for European monetary union would be met, but he added the debate over EMU would go on.
Speaking at the entrepreneurs' conference attended by Kohl, Stoiber said the chancellor had expressed "with greatest clarity" that the convergence criteria would be met.
Stoiber said a stable euro would be a great opportunity for the German and the European economy. Stoiber said he would not be meeting Kohl to discuss the issue.

In Tokyo, Gerd Haeusler, a member of the management board at Dresdner Bank warned about flight of capital if nations were to rush ahead and launch the euro on time even though nations are not yet fully ready to permanently link their currencies.

"I personally consider it a risk if monetary union were to be commenced without fundamental reform of economic policy being irrevocably launched in the countries seeking membership (in Europe's currency union)," he said.
"It would be risky to give priority to the timetable for monetary union over the fulfilment of the criteria," he added.

Luxembourg Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker criticised the euro debate in Germany over how strictly the EMU entry criteria should be interpreted. Juncker told Germany's MDR radio the discussion underscoring a growing rift between Kohl's CDU and Stoiber's CSU was damaging for the project.
He was speaking on the day his country took over the rotating European Union presidency.
"I find this German discussion unhealthy," Juncker said.
